title: Mechanistic primer on residual streams
body:
# Mechanistic primer on residual streams

Notes from working through the basics. The residual stream is the bus everything else writes to and reads from — attention heads add their weighted-sum contributions, MLPs add their feature transformations, and the final layer norm + unembed translates to logits. Every layer's contribution is *additive* in this sense, which is why steering vectors work at all.

Two things I keep forgetting:
- Layer index matters enormously. Early layers carry surface lexical structure; mid layers carry abstract concepts; late layers carry task-specific output preparation. Pick the wrong layer for a probe and you measure the wrong thing.
- Aggregation is not innocent. Mean-pooling residual stream activations across tokens loses positional structure. Last-token pooling assumes the final token has aggregated everything — usually true for autoregressive models, sometimes false. Decide before you measure.

The thing nobody mentions in the textbooks: when you sum residual contributions you're implicitly assuming a kind of distributional commutativity. Two heads contributing to the same direction is reinforcement; two heads contributing in opposite directions is cancellation; two heads contributing in nearly-orthogonal directions is genuine compositional encoding. Linear probes can't distinguish these cases. You need higher-order structure to see the difference, which is why nonlinear methods keep finding things linear ones miss.

This connects back to a thing Marcus said about factor portfolios: *"the second-order structure is where the alpha lives. First-order is everyone."* Same shape.

title: Why SAEs miss helices
body:
# Why SAEs miss helices

Working through the duality argument. Sparse autoencoders are *trained* to find sparse linear factorisations. That training objective imposes a prior: every concept has an independent direction, the directions tile the activation space, and a small number of directions explain any given activation.

The problem is that human concepts are not always shaped that way. Days of the week sit on a circle. Months sit on a circle. The concept "September" is not orthogonal to "August" or "October" — it lives geometrically *between* them. An SAE trained on residual stream activations will find directions that *correlate* with each month, but the directions are shards of the underlying ring rather than the ring itself. Steering along any one direction takes you off the ring into the void.

This generalises. Any concept with a periodic, helical, or cyclically-coupled structure is going to get shattered by SAEs. Years of a century → helix. Hours of a day → circle. Emotional valence-arousal space → roughly elliptical surface. Social roles → shells in some power-warmth axis pair. The interpretability tool you pick determines what you can see. If your only tool is sparse linear directions, you only see things that decompose linearly.

The implication for retrieval is direct: if I'm trying to find conceptual neighbours of a note that's "about Septembers" in some sense, an SAE-derived neighbourhood metric will treat any month as roughly equally close. A geometrically faithful method should know September is *between* August and October on the manifold. Whether anyone's built that retrieval method yet is the open question.

Compare to factor models in finance: the principal-components-style decomposition assumes orthogonal factors. But economic regimes interact — credit and rates aren't independent, they're coupled through risk appetite. Linear factor decomposition misses the coupling. Same family of mistakes.

title: Interpretability fellowship application — draft notes
body:
# Interpretability fellowship application — draft notes

Drafting the statement of purpose. Three things I want to communicate:

**1. What I'd build, given a fellowship slot.** A retrieval system over a personal knowledge base that uses activation-derived geometry rather than text embeddings. The hypothesis is that cross-domain conceptual bridges live in the curved structure of model activations and are systematically lost by cosine retrieval over flat embedding vectors. Falsifiable in a week with a small benchmark.

**2. Why this isn't just a feature.** If the hypothesis lands, it's a primitive — a portable representation of conceptual position usable across any knowledge tool, not just my notes. If it doesn't land, the empirical falsifier is published anyway and the field knows one more thing.

**3. What I'd need.** A modest GPU budget for activation extraction across a few open-source models, an academic advisor familiar with the recent geometry-zoo work, and time. The corpus and queries are already in shape.

The risk of this kind of project — Marcus pointed it out at lunch — is the seduction of the framing. "Geometry of meaning" is a beautiful phrase that's also done a lot of philosophical work for projects that didn't have measurement underneath. I need to lead with the falsifier, not the framing. Describe the bench first, the philosophy second.

What I keep coming back to: the strongest version of any speculative project is the one where you can describe the experiment that would refute it and you'd actually update on the result. If I can't articulate that, I haven't earned the fellowship.

title: Linear vs nonlinear concept geometry — survey notes
body:
# Linear vs nonlinear concept geometry — survey notes

Reading list and observations.

**Linear representation hypothesis (Park, Jiang, et al.)**: concepts in language models are encoded as directions in activation space. Steering by adding a direction shifts the output along that concept axis. Empirically supported for many concepts — sentiment, gender, nationality.

**Where it breaks**: as soon as the concept has internal structure (cyclic, hierarchical, ordinal-but-not-linear), the linear story stops capturing what the model actually does. Geodesic interpolation experiments show models stay coherent when steering follows the manifold's curve, and break when steering cuts through the void between curve segments.

**Goodfire's geometry zoo**: circles for periodic concepts, helices for years, Fourier features in specific neurons performing actual sinusoidal transforms, shells for social roles, quadrants for moral concepts, phylogenetic trees for biological taxa. The geometry isn't speculative — it's recoverable with the right tools.

**The duality (Hindupur–Lubana–Fel–Ba 2025)**: SAEs impose structural priors that determine what concepts can be detected. Different SAE architectures see different things. There's no neutral interpretability tool — every method is a question, and every question shapes the answer.

**Open question for me**: does this matter for retrieval? Or is it strictly a control / steering concern? My intuition is it does matter, because retrieval is implicitly a "find things on the same manifold neighbourhood" operation, and the neighbourhood structure is what curvature changes. But I have to prove it on a benchmark or it stays intuition.

The pattern across all of this is a shift from *"concepts are points"* to *"concepts are positions on a structured surface."* That second framing is more expensive to work with — non-Euclidean, often non-stationary — but appears to track what models actually do. The cost is justified if the downstream tasks reward respecting the structure.

title: Activation steering experiments — daily log
body:
# Activation steering experiments — daily log

**2026-04-29** — Set up TransformerLens against Gemma 3 12B, residual stream hooks at layer 18 (mid-network). Steered toward "playful" by averaging activations from 50 prompts containing the concept and subtracting a neutral baseline. Got the expected shift in tone. Sanity check passed.

**2026-04-30** — Tried to steer toward "Tuesday." Got incoherent output around the steering coefficient sweep. Direct evidence of the geodesic-vs-linear thing: Tuesday is on a circle (days of week), and pushing along the linear average direction takes you off the circle into the void. Distribution becomes ill-defined. Had to back off the coefficient by 4× to recover coherent output.

**2026-05-01** — Replicated on Llama 3.1 8B with the same prompt set. Same failure mode. Cross-architecture stability of the failure suggests it's a property of the underlying manifold, not the specific model. Logging this as positive evidence the day-of-week ring is a real geometric structure rather than a quirk of one model.

**2026-05-04** — Started writing up a small note for the personal corpus. Realised mid-draft that the "geodesic interpolation stays coherent" claim from the talk needs a more rigorous test than I've done — I've shown linear steering breaks; I haven't shown geodesic steering doesn't. Need to actually fit a geodesic to the day-of-week ring and steer along it. Saved as a Crucible task for next week.

**Pattern**: every steering experiment that doesn't respect existing structure fails predictably. Every one that does respect it works mundanely. The interesting science isn't in the failures — it's in *which structures the model actually maintains internally vs which we project onto it.* That's the difference between manifold cartography and apophenia.

title: Quant track vs ML research — fork analysis
body:
# Quant track vs ML research — fork analysis

The decision I keep deferring. Ten years in systematic equity has been good — Meridian is a solid shop, the work is intellectually live, the comp is fine. But the *next* ten years feel uncertain in a way the last ten didn't.

**The quant track from here**:
- Promotion path is clear: senior researcher → desk lead → CIO of strategy. Three to five-year horizon to the desk lead level.
- Comp continues compounding well. $X to ~$2X over 5 years if I execute.
- Skill compounding *in the field* is real. I'm noticeably better at this than I was at the 5-year mark.
- Risk: factor-decay dynamics mean systematic equity at firms my size becomes structurally harder over time. The desk-lead role at year 35 may not be doing what the desk-lead role at year 25 does.

**The ML research track**:
- Possible entry via interpretability or RL for finance. Goodfire, Anthropic, OpenAI all have non-academic research roles.
- Massive credential gap. No PhD, no published papers (yet — the geodesic work could become one). Means starting at IC level despite seniority elsewhere.
- Comp would drop materially in the first 2-3 years. Meridian's RSU + performance comp doesn't translate.
- But: the 10-year skill-compounding curve is at the start of the steep section, not the flat. The thing I learn in year 1 of ML research is much more than the thing I learn in year 11 of systematic equity.
- Risk: I might just be wrong about my own ability to make the transition. Mid-career switches are notoriously survivor-biased — the success stories you read are not a fair sample.

**The hybrid path** (least defined): keep the day job, ship the geodesic-retrieval bench publicly, see if anyone in the ML research world reaches out. Convert the interest into a part-time advisory or sabbatical-research role, then re-evaluate. Optionality preserving.

**What Marcus said when I floated this**: "The question isn't which track has higher expected value. Both are reasonable lives. The question is: which version of you do you want to be at 60? You answer that, the path picks itself."

**Working answer**: hybrid path for 12 months. Ship the bench. See who notices. Re-evaluate at the year mark.

**The discomfort I keep noticing**: this is a long-cycle decision being made under heavy short-cycle noise (recent quarter at Meridian was great → "stay!"; a frustrating week at Meridian → "leave!"). The decision quality has to come from the structural reasoning, not from how this week went. Hard to internalise.

title: Mentor sessions with Marcus — 2026 Q1
body:
# Mentor sessions with Marcus — 2026 Q1

Quarterly check-in with Marcus over a long lunch on the Sunshine Coast. Capturing the threads while fresh.

**On the geodesic-retrieval project**: he's sceptical of the framing but interested in the falsifier. Specifically pushed back on "the geometry isn't in the network, it's in the world" — calls it overreach. His version: "What you're testing is whether activation-derived neighbourhoods are operationally more useful than embedding-derived neighbourhoods. That's a worthy question. Don't dress it up as cosmology." Fair. Adjusted my own framing as a result.

**On the Meridian fork**: he's been through the equivalent (left a similar shop at 38 to do something more open-ended; has visible regret about *some* of how that went, but not the choice itself). His specific advice: "Don't optimise for which path is better. Optimise for which one you can stay curious about for ten years. The curiosity dominates the comp differential at any reasonable horizon." Same shape as his earlier "which version of you do you want to be at 60" framing.

**On Caspian / riding**: Marcus rides too — used to event seriously, now mostly trail. Spent fifteen minutes on the geometry of the half-pass, which he thinks I've been over-thinking. His view: stop trying to *engineer* the lateral aids; let the rhythm carry the movement. Actionable; took it to Priya, who agreed.

**Marcus's frame I keep stealing**: "The world has fewer experts than you think and the experts have less to teach you than you think. The thing that compounds is your own attention to the work — *how* you look at it, not *who* tells you how to look at it." Said in the context of why he stopped going to industry conferences. Will probably feel different to me at his age.

**Action items from the session**:
- Send him the Projecting Assumptions paper reference. He doesn't track interpretability literature but the duality argument might land.
- Set up a coffee with his old colleague who's at OpenAI — speculative networking but Marcus thinks the conversation is worth having.
- Get my desk's regime-detection model to a stage where Marcus can review it. He's the best critic for that work I have access to.

**Pattern noticed**: Marcus is one of two people in my life whose advice consistently improves the *quality of my questions* rather than answering them directly. Priya is the other. The high-leverage relationships are with people who reframe; the lower-leverage ones are with people who advise.

title: Negotiation prep — equity vs cash
body:
# Negotiation prep — equity vs cash

Annual review prep for late June. Working through what I want to ask for and what I'd accept.

**Current package**: base + bonus structure with a 70/30 cash split. Vested equity in Meridian's GP — small but real exposure to firm-level performance. Total comp last year ~$X (target).

**What I want for next cycle**:
1. **Higher equity allocation, lower cash**. The cash is more than I need at the current marginal-tax rate. Marginal $1 of equity has more long-run expected value than marginal $1 of cash, given my belief Meridian is structurally well-positioned for the next 5 years. Specifically: ask for 50/50 instead of 70/30.
2. **Carve-out for my external research**. Want explicit written permission to publish work outside Meridian's IP umbrella, on the geodesic-retrieval line specifically. Not asking for time off; asking for non-encumbrance.
3. **Sabbatical option vested at year 12**. Currently no formal sabbatical. Would accept a $X reduction in cash comp in exchange for a guaranteed 3-month sabbatical in 2028.

**The firm's likely concerns**:
- (1) is fine — Meridian wants partners with skin in the game, not arbitrageable employees. They'll counter on the *delta* (50/50 too aggressive; 60/40 likely).
- (2) is the sticky one. IP umbrella is broad and the firm has had problems with employees publishing things that could be argued to use firm-developed signals. I'll need to specifically describe the scope (interpretability research, not investment research) and accept a review process.
- (3) might surprise them but isn't unreasonable for a 12-year tenure. Frame as retention; don't apologise for it.

**My BATNA**: I'd be employable elsewhere at similar comp without much friction. Goldman Sachs Asset Management's systematic team has been recruiting; so has Citadel. The walk-away rate isn't bluff — it's just expensive enough that I won't trigger it lightly.

**The ask I keep almost forgetting**: better deferred-compensation structure. Currently the bonus is paid in cash with a partial RSU lock. The lock structure is generous but the *timing* of cash flow doesn't suit my life — I'd rather defer more, take more in equity, less liquidity now. This is essentially free for the firm and meaningful to me.

**Negotiation discipline**: do not anchor on dollar amounts in the first conversation. Anchor on *structure* (equity %, IP carve-out, sabbatical). The dollar amounts follow from the structure. Anchoring on dollars first is how junior negotiations go badly — you get a number that fits the existing structure rather than the structure you wanted.

**Note for next year**: write this kind of memo *before* the meeting, not after, every year. Last year I went in with vibes and got vibes-quality outcomes.

title: Conference circuit — ROI estimates
body:
# Conference circuit — ROI estimates

Reviewing which conferences are worth attending in the back half of 2026. The default answer ("attend the ones I attended last year") is lazy. Trying to do this with explicit reasoning.

**The question**: what does a conference give me that I couldn't get from reading the proceedings + a few targeted DMs?

**Things conferences provide that text doesn't**:
1. Hallway conversations with researchers I wouldn't have warm intros to. Real, irreplaceable. The structured talks are usually the *least* valuable hour on the conference's schedule.
2. Compressed signal about the field's current taste. What's hot, what's tired, what's quietly being abandoned. Hard to read from papers because papers lag the consensus by 12 months.
3. Forced context-switching out of my daily mental modes. Sometimes the most useful thing about a conference is being away from Brisbane for four days and physically tired enough to think differently.

**Things conferences pretend to provide but don't**:
1. Talks I "couldn't have read at home." For 90% of talks, the recording or paper is sufficient.
2. Networking for the sake of networking. Random small talk produces 1% follow-throughs at best. The valuable connections happen at dinners with already-warm contacts, not at booth-area chats.

**The 2026 candidates and my read**:
- **NeurIPS** (December, San Diego). High signal density on interpretability tracks given the geodesic-retrieval angle. Probably yes; need to angle for at least 2 dinner/coffee meetings with Goodfire-adjacent researchers to make the trip pay off.
- **ICML** (July, Vancouver). Moderate. Less interpretability-focused than NeurIPS. Probably skip unless someone I want to meet is there.
- **Quant industry conference** (September, NYC). I usually attend. This year: skip. The industry conferences have flattened — same speakers, same takes, low surprise. Spend the time on Crucible instead.
- **Local Brisbane ML meetup**. Free. 1 hour/month. Yes — costs nothing, occasionally produces a useful contact.

**The accidental conference**: there's a small interpretability workshop being put on by a Sydney-based researcher in October. ~30 attendees, day-and-a-half format. The signal-to-noise on these tiny events is usually 5× higher than big conferences. Going.

**Pattern**: the right strategy for conferences is the inverse of what most people do. Skip the big-name events with too many people; lean into the small focused workshops where everyone in the room actually cares. Same logic as buying small-cap value vs large-cap growth — less liquid, more mispricing, higher real return.

title: Reading list — strategic thinking
body:
# Reading list — strategic thinking

Building this list slowly. The goal is books I'd recommend to someone earlier in their career who wanted to develop better long-horizon judgment, not "leadership."

**Already read, kept on the active reread list**:
- *Seeing Like a State* — Scott. The single most useful book I've read on the costs of legibility. Applies directly to risk modelling: every legible model imposes a partition on the underlying reality, and the partition has costs the model can't see.
- *Reality Has a Surprising Amount of Detail* — Mollick (essay). Short but I reread quarterly. The argument: the gap between "knowing a thing" and "doing a thing" is usually filled with details that are invisible until you try.
- *Antifragile* — Taleb. Yes, the man's tone is what it is. The framing of "what gains from disorder" still earns its keep when thinking about risk.
- *On the Heart* — Hadot's collected essays. Stoic philosophy as practice rather than doctrine.

**Currently reading**:
- *The Body Keeps the Score* — van der Kolk. Slow read. Mainstream but useful for the somatic-attention thread I keep returning to. Connects to the riding-as-attention-training arc.
- *Probably Approximately Correct* — Valiant. Foundational, occasionally heavy. Worth working through carefully.

**Working queue**:
- *Range* — Epstein. Heard the argument secondhand many times; want to read primary.
- *The Knowledge Illusion* — Sloman & Fernbach. On the social distribution of knowledge.
- *Trust* — Lou Marinoff (philosophical, not the pop one). Thicker treatment than the management-book version.

**What I keep noticing reading these**: the books that hold up over rereads are the ones with operative *frames* rather than *checklists*. *Seeing Like a State* gives me a way to look at any system; the frame works in domains Scott never wrote about. Whereas books with checklists ("the 7 habits of...") tend to atrophy fast — the checklist either becomes habit and recedes, or doesn't and you stop using it.

**The reading discipline I'm trying to keep**: one fiction book for every two non-fiction. The fiction shapes my prose and my pattern recognition in ways nonfiction doesn't. Currently reading Le Guin's *The Dispossessed* slowly. The economics of Anarres holds up better than most economics textbooks.

**The book I keep promising myself I'll write**: a quant-trader's guide to attention. Not a how-to. A frame. The stoic practice section, the somatic attention texture stuff, the regime-conditional inference parallel between trading and riding. Maybe the geodesic-retrieval project is part of the same arc, just expressed in code instead of prose.

title: Daily — 2026-04-15
body:
# Daily — 2026-04-15

Up at 6:10. Went to the arena at 7 — Caspian was unsettled (a new horse arrived yesterday, the herd dynamic is rebalancing). Did 20 minutes of in-hand work to bring his attention back; abandoned the planned ridden session. *Right call* — pushing through wouldn't have produced learning, only resistance.

Drove to Meridian. The morning model run flagged the materials sector for an unusual position size. Spent the first hour validating — turned out to be a stale data feed from one of the alt-data providers. Fixed by switching the feed; sector position normalised. The alarm worked. Kept logs.

Lunch with Robin near Brunswick Street. She's been working on a string-quartet recording in a studio in West End — interesting reflection from her about the difference between *take 1* (raw, often best) and *take 4* (technically clean but loses the spark). Same dynamic as my own writing. The first draft has the energy; the polished one is correct but flatter. Worth thinking about how to keep some of the take-1 quality through revisions.

Afternoon: deep work on the regime-detection ensemble. The Bayesian online changepoint detector is too noisy by itself; the ensemble approach is converging. Spent 90 minutes reading through Adams & MacKay's original paper to understand what's happening when it spuriously flags. The math is clearer when read carefully than when remembered.

Evening: Robin practising scales (she keeps her practice texture *very* different from my work mode — slow, repetitive, almost meditative). Cooked. Read 30 pages of *The Body Keeps the Score*.

**Bed**. The day had structure; not all do. Notice the days that don't and try to engineer them. The reliable cadence — morning movement, deep-work block, light evening — is what makes the cumulative work compound. The days I lose to scattered attention bleed into the next day, and three of those in a row halve the week's output.

Slept badly. Woke at 4:30, couldn't get back. Morning ride was inadvisable in retrospect — I went anyway. Caspian read me as not-quite-there and the session was mediocre. Should have gone for a walk instead. Note for the rule book: if sleep is below 6 hours, swap arena for a hack. Don't try to teach.

Marcus pinged with an article about Lubana's Projecting Assumptions paper — coincidence or he's been paying attention to my project. Either way, useful prompt.

Spent an hour over coffee thinking about the geodesic-retrieval bench design. The cross-domain-bridge query format is the hard part. Easy to write a query that's *obvious* (which fails the manifold-test because cosine handles it). Easy to write a query that's *random* (which fails because there is no real bridge). The query I want is *non-obvious but real* — and constructing those requires me to actually know the corpus deeply. Which means I should keep the corpus small enough that I can hold it in my head.

Caspian's insurance renewal landed in the email. Reminded me to actually do the spreadsheet I keep meaning to. Set a calendar block for Saturday morning.

Evening: read Hadot's chapter on Marcus Aurelius's *praemeditatio*. The exposure-therapy framing keeps landing for me. Wrote a longer note on it.

**Reflection**: the deferral pattern I keep noticing — small admin tasks slip below the threshold of attention and pile up. The energy review, the insurance review, the body-corporate dispute, all sit in a queue I don't process unless I make explicit time. The cost is small per item and large in aggregate. Saturday-morning audit ritual? Possibly.

Riding session in the afternoon — finally a clean shoulder-in to the right. Eight months of work, mostly on my own posture. The breakthrough wasn't in the exercise itself; it was in the cumulative postural work over weeks that finally let the cue land cleanly. *The improvement compounds invisibly until it doesn't.*

Robin's quartet had a recording session that ran late. Cooked alone. Watched the last episode of a Korean drama she's been watching with me — paused on the philosophical thread in the writing. The scriptwriter was clearly working with stoic ideas without ever naming them. Recurring theme: the protagonists who survive are the ones who pre-rehearsed loss; the ones who didn't break under unexpected stress.

Posted a small thread about activation steering experiments to a small interpretability mailing list. Got two thoughtful replies within an hour. The signal-to-noise on small lists is *enormously* better than on the big platforms.

**Reflection on the quarter**: the slow compound of work shows up at quarter-end aggregations in a way it doesn't show up daily. The factor decay was visible quarterly. The riding breakthrough was visible quarterly. The relationship with Marcus, the geodesic project, all of it accumulates more legibly when reviewed at this cadence than at the daily one. Keep the quarterly review ritual.

Long weekend. Used the morning to actually do the insurance comparison spreadsheet I've been putting off for two months. Three takeaways:

Note for the systems library: build a quarterly admin ritual that *includes* small math-based decisions, so the leverage is salient.

Afternoon: long walk along the Brisbane River with Robin. Weather perfect. The river reach near the New Farm peninsula was surprisingly empty — usually it's busier on long weekends. Worth remembering for next year.

Evening: started a draft of the README for the geodesic-retrieval project. Will need to revise heavily — first drafts always have the wrong tone for me, too philosophical. Ben Caughlin's recent reshape of his Flywheel Geometry repo is a good reference point — measurement-first framing, the cosmological frame moved to a separate philosophy.md. I should steal the structure.

Read the next two chapters of *The Dispossessed*. Le Guin's economics on Anarres is the weirdest sustained thought experiment in fiction I've read; the part where the protagonist tries to explain "ownership" to people who literally don't have the concept is the most useful piece of writing about coordination problems I know. Saving a few quotes.

**Reflection**: long weekends are not really for rest; they're for the work that requires uninterrupted hours. I do my best thinking on Saturdays and Sundays. Mid-week is for execution. The shape of my week wants this asymmetry — accept it, design for it, stop pretending I'll do good thinking on a Tuesday at 4pm.

title: Caspian — horse profile
body:
# Caspian — horse profile

8-year-old Andalusian gelding. Dappled grey, full mane, 16.1hh. Bought from a small breeder in the Lockyer Valley three years ago. Currently stabled at Kenmore Equestrian, working with Priya weekly.

**Temperament**: forward but not hot. Reads handler energy quickly — calibration of my own state matters more than any technique I apply. If I come to the arena tense from Meridian, he picks it up in the first five minutes and we lose the whole session. If I show up centred, he settles within minutes and we get real work done.

**Strengths**: lateral movement (especially shoulder-in and travers), uphill canter, willingness to engage on small cues. Picks up new exercises in 2–3 sessions if introduced cleanly.

**Weaknesses**: tendency to anticipate and offer the previous figure rather than wait for the cue. Hollows under pressure. Cold-back issue in winter — needs a 10-minute walk warmup before any contact, no exceptions.

**Training arc**: started in groundwork and long-lining, worked up to first-level dressage tests. Currently building toward a flying change. The change has been a 6-month project — most of the difficulty isn't physical, it's the calibration of straightness and balance going into the canter aid. Get those right and the change happens almost incidentally.

**The thing I keep relearning**: every time I think I'm training Caspian, I'm also being trained. He's a feedback system that punishes inconsistency immediately and rewards calibrated input. Working with him has changed how I think about quantitative model design. Both are about calibration, both are about reading distributional signals correctly, both have a tail-risk regime where small mis-calibrations compound into refusals or losses.

title: Lateral work session 2026-04-12
body:
# Lateral work session 2026-04-12

Worked shoulder-in down both long sides, then alternated shoulder-in / travers in 10m circles. 50 minutes total. Priya supervising.

**What worked**: the rhythm-first approach. Once I stopped trying to angle Caspian before establishing tempo, the lateral movement happened almost by itself. The cue I think is "create the shoulder-in" is actually "create the rhythm cleanly enough that the shoulder-in is the path of least resistance."

**What didn't**: shoulder-in to the right is still notably worse than to the left. He hollows on the right rein, drops the right shoulder, and rushes. Working theory: I unconsciously brace through my right hip when riding right, which transmits as conflicting cues. Priya thinks it's me, not him.

**Pattern observed**: there's a regime change in his way of going around minute 25. Before that, he's offering compliant but mechanical work. After 25 minutes of correct rhythm and consistent cues, he switches to *offering* — anticipating the next shoulder-in, lifting his back, taking the contact forward. Same horse, same exercises, completely different feel. The transition is sharp, not gradual. Something about cumulative consistency tipping him into a more engaged state.

**Connection point**: this maps onto something I see in factor portfolios. Sometimes the position works mechanically for weeks — small positive carry, no surprises — and then suddenly the regime shifts and the same position starts paying differently. Same trade, same exposure, completely different return character. The shift is sharp, not gradual. In both cases, the lever isn't the action — it's the consistency of conditions that causes a phase change in the underlying dynamics.

**For next session**: address the right-rein bracing. Maybe ride with no contact on the right rein for 5 minutes to feel where I'm interfering. Priya suggested off-horse stretching for the right hip flexor too.

title: Exploration vs exploitation in groundwork
body:
# Exploration vs exploitation in groundwork

The horse-training literature is mostly *exploitation* literature — exercises proven to produce specific outcomes, drilled until reliable. There's a quieter strand of training thinking that's about *exploration* — letting the horse offer behaviours you didn't ask for, then noticing which ones to reinforce.

The tension is real. Pure exploitation produces a reliable but brittle horse — works the cued exercises, panics outside the trained envelope. Pure exploration produces a curious horse with no reliable cues. Neither extreme is what I want.

What seems to work is **scheduled exploration**. 80% of every session is structured: warmup, planned exercises, cool-down. 20% is open-ended — I cue an idea and wait without insisting, see what Caspian offers. Sometimes nothing. Sometimes he offers something I didn't think of: a transition I hadn't planned, a willingness to bend in a direction I hadn't asked for. Those moments are gold and I write them down.

The mathematical analogy is the explore/exploit tradeoff in bandit problems and in RL. Greedy policies converge fast but get trapped in local optima. ε-greedy explores enough to find better policies. The 80/20 in groundwork is essentially ε ≈ 0.2, except the "rewards" being explored aren't just behaviours — they're the *shape of the relationship between handler and horse*. You're searching policy space and rapport space simultaneously.

This connects to something Marcus said about research careers: "Drill the technique you have, but reserve a fraction of your time for problems your technique doesn't solve. The drilled fraction pays the rent. The exploration fraction is where the next ten years come from." Same shape.

What I'd love to find: a principled way to know when to up ε. With Caspian, I think it's when the planned exercises become *too* automatic — the relationship is fine but stops compounding. Same diagnostic with research: when the work is getting easier but not more interesting, push exploration up.

title: Reading the horse's energy — calibration notes
body:
# Reading the horse's energy — calibration notes

Priya's been pushing me on this for a year. The phrase "reading his energy" sounds woo until you take it seriously as a *measurement problem*.

What I'm actually doing when I "read his energy": integrating multiple low-bandwidth signals over time. Ear position. Whether the lower jaw is soft or set. Whether his back rounds under my seat or stays flat. The depth of his breathing. The cadence of his footfalls. None of these signals individually carry much information. Combined and tracked over time, they're a high-precision posterior over his current state.

The calibration is in *which combination* signals what. A horse can have flickering ears and be relaxed (just attentive). A horse can have set ears and be relaxed (just hot day, conserving energy). The signals are conditionally informative — you have to know the joint distribution.

What I've found is that I'm a fairly bad calibrator on this for the first 10 minutes of any session, much better by minute 30. There's something about the tuning of my attention that takes warmup time. Possibly I'm establishing a baseline distribution against which deviations become legible.

**Risk-model parallel**: the same pattern shows up in regime detection. Static thresholds (volatility above X, correlation below Y) are weak. Conditional thresholds calibrated against a recent rolling baseline are much stronger. My morning model that's been running on yesterday's distribution catches regime changes faster than one re-fit cold every morning. The warmup matters.

**Practical implication**: I should stop expecting clean signal in the first 10 minutes of a ride. Treat that period as calibration, not as work. Note the baseline. Then start asking for things, with the prior in place to detect when something shifts off it.

The deeper point is that "reading energy" isn't mystical. It's just a name for high-bandwidth conditional inference under partial observability. Riding sharpens skills that show up everywhere. My quant intuition has gotten better since I started taking groundwork seriously, and I don't think that's coincidence.

title: Trailer loading reset training plan
body:
# Trailer loading reset training plan

Caspian had a bad experience at a clinic in February — got off-balance during a hill descent and now associates the trailer with the moment of fear. He'll load if pushed but only with significant resistance. Need to reset the association before our next event in June.

**Diagnosis**: not a training problem; an emotional learning problem. The mechanics of loading are fine. The aversion is in the anticipated trajectory, not the act.

**Reset protocol** (drawn from Warwick Schiller's approach, adapted):

1. **Week 1**: trailer parked in the arena, doors open, no expectation of loading. Walk past it during normal sessions. Let him sniff. No food bribery — that creates a different conditioning loop and confuses the signal.
2. **Week 2**: invite approach without insisting. Hold him on the lead, walk *near* the ramp, walk away if he looks tense, return when he relaxes. The repetition of "near, then leaving" decouples proximity from threat.
3. **Week 3**: invite a single foot on the ramp. Reward by walking off, not by pushing further. Repeat until he offers two feet, three, four. The progression is *his* not mine.
4. **Week 4**: full loading, but treat the inside of the trailer as a place to hang out, not a corridor to a destination. Stand inside with him for 5 minutes, then unload. Repeat.
5. **Week 5+**: reintroduce short journeys on flat ground, gradually increasing length, never repeating the hill profile that caused the original event until much later.

**Underlying principle**: the original aversion was a Bayesian update. The reset is *also* a series of Bayesian updates. You can't argue with the prior; you can only feed it new evidence in a way it can integrate. Forcing it through the trailer would just generate more aversive evidence and reinforce the wrong association.

**Connection**: the same principle applies to model calibration after a regime break. Once a strategy has been shocked by an out-of-sample event, you can't just keep running it — every drawdown reinforces the bad updates the model is doing. You need to feed it a controlled stream of recoverable conditions until the model's belief about its own competence rebuilds. Backtest the equivalent of the trailer parked in the arena. Then trade small. Then scale.

title: Quarterly tax estimate Q1 2026
body:
# Quarterly tax estimate Q1 2026

Australian PAYG instalments + the side-income reconciliation. Doing this myself this quarter rather than handing to the accountant — partly to keep tax-current cognition active, partly because the side income from a small consulting engagement adds complexity my accountant takes a week to bill for.

**Income components** (Q1 2026):
- Meridian salary + Q4 bonus (paid in Q1) — tax already withheld, mostly straightforward.
- Small consulting fee from a Melbourne fund — paid as ABN income, GST applicable. ~$8,400 incl GST.
- Investment dividends — Australian sourced, franking credits to capture.
- Foreign dividends from one US ETF — withholding to claim back via the tax treaty.

**Estimated PAYG instalment**: ATO calculator gives a number based on prior year's tax. The number this quarter is misleading because the consulting income won't continue at the same rate. Need to vary the instalment using the variation form, otherwise I overpay and chase the refund later. Decision: vary downward by 30%.

**The franking credit detail**: most retail investors miss this. Australian dividends carry franking credits — pre-paid tax at the corporate level. When I receive the dividend, I can claim the franking credit against my own tax liability. On a $1,000 fully-franked dividend, I get $1,000 cash + ~$430 franking credit, taxed on the $1,430 grossed-up amount. Net effect: dividends are taxed at marginal-minus-corporate-rate, much friendlier than they appear at first glance.

**The conceptual point**: Australian tax has a dozen of these "look at the actual mechanics, not the surface number" gotchas. Foreign withholding, franking credits, division 7A, CGT discount thresholds. None of them are conceptually hard once you've worked through them once. The accountant value-add is mostly in *remembering* them when fatigue is high — not in the conceptual difficulty.

**Connection back to model design**: same shape as factor portfolio reporting. The headline returns hide implementation details (transaction costs, capacity constraints, tax drag) that materially change the picture. Reading only the headline is exactly the same kind of mistake as ignoring franking credits. The mature operator looks past the surface number every time.

**For next quarter**: build a simple spreadsheet that does the variation calculation automatically. The arithmetic isn't hard; the discipline is. Automate the discipline.

title: Body corporate disputes — strata notes
body:
# Body corporate disputes — strata notes

Apartment block has a body corporate / strata committee. Meets quarterly. Most of the work is benign but a recurring set of disputes keeps surfacing and they're worth thinking about as a pattern, not as individual problems.

**The current disputes**:
1. **Recurring water ingress in unit 7**. Three years running. Each time, the committee debates whether it's structural (common-property responsibility) or in-unit (owner's problem). Each time the answer is unclear, an inspection costs $1,200, and the conclusion is mealy. Real fix would require investigating the building envelope, which nobody wants to fund.
2. **Pool closure for "weather damage"** that's actually accumulated maintenance debt. The committee has been deferring real maintenance for 5 years; calling it weather damage gets the special-levy approved more easily than calling it neglect. Honesty would cost less but creates worse politics.
3. **Visitor parking abuse**. The bylaws are clear; enforcement is weak. The same three units violate consistently; the committee won't issue formal notices because two of the three are committee members.

**The structural problem**: the body corporate operates on consensus among self-interested parties with limited time. Decisions that would be obvious for a single rational owner — "fix the building envelope, raise levies, accept the cost" — never happen because the political cost to whichever committee member proposes it is unbounded. The system isn't broken; it's working as designed, and the design is weak.

**What I keep almost forgetting**: this is not unique to strata. Any decision-making body operating by consensus among self-interested parties with limited time has the same failure mode. Investment committees, academic department meetings, large families dividing inheritance. The pattern produces predictable underinvestment in maintenance and predictable preference for blame-shifting language ("weather damage") over honesty.

**The actionable takeaway**: in any such system, the leverage point is to *reduce the political cost of honest framing*. If "the pool needs a $40k overhaul because we deferred maintenance for 5 years" is politically punishing to say, the system stays stuck. If you can rework norms so that saying it is *expected*, the structure unblocks. Hard. Slow. The kind of work that takes years and is invisible until suddenly things start getting fixed.

**Connection to investing**: this is exactly the dynamic that makes corporate governance reform so slow. Boards, like strata committees, are consensus bodies of self-interested actors. The people best positioned to call out problems have the most to lose by doing so. The reform path is always cultural before procedural — change what's politically sayable, then the procedures follow.

title: Solar feed-in tariff renegotiation
body:
# Solar feed-in tariff renegotiation

Current feed-in tariff is 7c/kWh from Origin Energy. Was 12c when the system was installed in 2022. The tariff has stepped down twice. Wholesale electricity has not stepped down by the same margin. Net effect: I'm getting a worse deal each year while my neighbours' new installs lock in better rates than my old one.

**The mechanics of why this happens**: retailers offer high feed-in tariffs to acquire customers, then quietly step them down at contract renewal. The customer notices late or not at all. The economic surplus migrates from the customer (who can't easily switch given the lock-in costs) back to the retailer.

**My options**:
1. **Switch retailer**. AGL and EnergyAustralia are currently offering 11c. Switching cost: ~$80, annoying admin. Annual benefit on my export volume: ~$540. Clear win, except for the residual concern that the new rate also steps down within 18 months.
2. **Negotiate with Origin**. Threaten to switch, see what they offer. Ratchet effect on my side: they tend to match competitors when faced with a credible exit threat.
3. **Stay put, do nothing**. Lazy default. Costs ~$540/year more than option 1. Real money over 5 years.
4. **Get a battery**. ~$8,000 install. Stops me feeding cheaply-bought-back power into the grid; I store it and use it overnight instead. Payback period 6-7 years at current tariffs; less if grid prices rise.

**Decision tree**:
- If I get a satisfactory negotiated rate at Origin: stay (option 2).
- If Origin won't move: switch to AGL (option 1), revisit the battery question separately.

**What this exercise revealed**: I've been on autopilot for the energy bill for two years. The dollar amount per month is small enough that it doesn't trigger attention; the cumulative cost over a decade is the price of a decent overseas trip. The lesson generalises — recurring small costs slip below my attention threshold and accumulate. Worth a quarterly "audit the small recurring costs" review.

**Connection back to investing**: this is the household-finance analogue of the management-fee drag on a fund. 1% per year sounds small. Over 30 years it's most of your terminal wealth. Same shape — the small recurring leakage that's not salient enough to fix but compounds into the dominant cost. The discipline is the same: notice the drag, fix it, redirect the saved cash to actual returns.

**Action item**: schedule a 1-hour quarterly review of all recurring costs. First Sunday of each quarter. Audit subscriptions, utilities, insurance, fees. Compare to alternatives. Switch where the saving is worth the friction.

title: Dog walker rota — scheduling logic
body:
# Dog walker rota — scheduling logic

Robin's mother's whippet (Rufus) lives with us when the parents travel — usually three week-long stretches per year. The dog walker rota during those stretches is a small operational problem worth getting right.

**The constraints**:
- Rufus needs two walks daily, ~45 mins each.
- Both Robin and I work during the day; we can do morning and evening but not midday.
- Lunchtime walk handled by a dog walker (Sammy, freelance, $25/walk).
- Sammy has flexibility but also has other clients; need to book the rota a week ahead.
- The garden is fully fenced so short break-outs during the day are okay.

**The previous mess**: last year I tried to coordinate this ad-hoc by texting Sammy each morning. Hit two cancellations because Sammy was already booked. Switched to a weekly rota emailed every Sunday — fixed the coordination problem but introduced a different one: cancellations on my side (last-minute work meetings) created friction because Sammy had blocked the slot.

**The current system**:
- Sunday evening: send Sammy the week's slots (Mon–Fri 12:30 walks).
- Wednesday morning: confirm the back half of the week (Wed pm + Thu/Fri).
- Cancellation policy: full payment if I cancel within 24h, 50% if 24-48h, free if more than 48h. Built in to acknowledge that Sammy's time has block-out cost.

**What worked unexpectedly well**: writing down the cancellation policy made cancellations rarer. The discipline of looking at the calendar 48h ahead — to avoid the cancellation fee — produced more accurate calendar review than I'd otherwise do. Small skin-in-the-game forces small attention.

**What I keep noticing**: scheduling problems are usually constraint-satisfaction problems pretending to be people problems. The person dimension matters but the constraint dimension is more tractable. Once I had the constraint structure clear (Sammy's block-out cost, my cancellation rate, Rufus's walk requirements), the rota fell out of the constraints almost automatically.

**Connection elsewhere**: this is the same shape as scheduling research priorities. The "I should write this paper" decision is constraint-satisfaction (time, energy, deadline pressure, opportunity cost of alternatives) wearing the costume of a personal-priority decision. Treating it as the constraint-satisfaction problem it actually is produces faster, less guilty decisions than treating it as a values question.

**For the next dog-sitting stretch (April 2027)**: build the same rota a week in advance, as before. Add: a backup walker contact in case Sammy is sick, vetted in advance.

title: Insurance renewal comparison spreadsheet
body:
# Insurance renewal comparison spreadsheet

Annual insurance review. Building this comparison spreadsheet because each year I forget the methodology and have to reconstruct it.

**The portfolio**:
- Home contents (replacement value ~$140k)
- Building insurance (paid via body corporate, not directly)
- Polestar 2 — comprehensive
- Trek Powerfly — added rider on contents (more on this below)
- Caspian — third-party liability + vet/mortality cover
- Robin's instruments — separately scheduled on the contents policy
- Drone — covered as scheduled item
- Travel — annual multi-trip policy

**The comparison method**: rather than comparing premiums, compare *premiums divided by claim limit* per item. A policy with a $500 deductible and $50k limit on jewellery is fundamentally different from one with $0 deductible and $30k limit. Headline premium hides this.

**This year's findings**:
- The contents policy has been quietly raising the premium 9% per year while inflation runs ~4%. Real-terms premium has compounded materially. Going to shop this.
- Polestar comprehensive is competitive — three quotes within 5% of each other; staying with current insurer.
- The Trek e-bike rider on contents is *underpriced* by the insurer (they don't fully understand e-bikes' actual replacement cost; my $7k bike is being insured at category rates that assume <$3k). Will not call attention to this. The mismatch is in my favour, will let it run until renewal asks the right question.
- The horse mortality cover is the line item I most underestimated. Premium = 4% of insured value annually. Over a horse's working life that's 30%+ of his value paid in premiums. Consider self-insuring the mortality piece (keep the third-party liability, drop mortality, save ~$1,800/year). Calculation: am I better off paying the premium or holding $40k in a separate sinking fund? Probably the sinking fund — the expected annual cost of mortality below the insurer's loaded premium.

**The pattern**: insurance is a portfolio of small leverage trades on tail events. Each trade has a premium-vs-payout ratio. The headline question — "is the premium reasonable?" — only matters in light of the payout structure. The shopper who looks only at premium gets adverse-selected by the insurer.

**The discipline that produces good outcomes**: a small once-yearly spreadsheet exercise comparing apples to apples. Most people don't do this; insurers love it. The rate at which premiums creep up is bounded only by how much friction it would take you to leave.

**Action item**: complete the contents shop by end of week. Decision on horse mortality self-insurance by end of month.

title: On the texture of attention
body:
# On the texture of attention

A thing I've been turning over: attention isn't a single quantity, it's a *texture*. There's the wide diffuse attention of scanning a market open — many things at low resolution. There's the narrow point attention of debugging a specific factor model bug. There's the rhythmic alternating attention of riding — the cycle of contact, release, contact, release. There's the back-of-mind attention that keeps a problem alive for days while you do other things.

These are different physiological states, and they're not interchangeable. Trying to debug a model with the diffuse attention you use for market opens is hopeless. Trying to scan markets with debugging-attention misses everything peripheral.

The thing nobody tells you in training as a quant is that *picking the right attention texture is a meta-skill*. The visible job is the analytic work; the invisible job is constantly re-tuning the kind of attention you're bringing.

What I've noticed is that the texture-tuning is often somatic before it's cognitive. Tense shoulders → you've been doing point-attention too long. Slack jaw → you're back in diffuse mode whether you wanted to be or not. The body is the interface to the attention texture, not the cognition. You shape attention by changing posture, breath, muscular tension.

Riding made this obvious in a way nothing else has. Caspian responds to my attention texture before he responds to any cue I'm consciously giving. If I'm carrying tight point-attention from a stressful market session, he reads "controlled, narrow, unsafe" and reacts. If I shift into rhythmic alternating attention before mounting, he reads "centred, communicative" and we have a chance.

**The deeper claim**: every kind of skilled performance has its own attention-texture signature, and improving in any field is partly the discovery of which texture serves the work. The texture isn't separable from the technique. Coaches who teach posture and breath instead of "concentrate harder" are quietly teaching texture-shaping.

This isn't woo. It's the operational physiology of attention. Eventually I'd like to see this written down in a way that doesn't trigger the *eye-roll reflex* in serious-thinking people. Possibly there's a quantitative version waiting somewhere in the EEG / heart-rate-variability literature, but the experiential reality is solid regardless.

title: What craftsmen know about feedback
body:
# What craftsmen know about feedback

Reading a chapter on tool use among Japanese carpenters. The thing that struck me: their training isn't only about technique. It's about the *quality of feedback* the tool gives.

A sharp chisel cuts cleanly and leaves a surface that *tells you* whether your angle was right. A dull chisel tears, but the tear hides whatever your angle did. So the apprentice's first job — for years — is sharpening. Not because dull chisels can't cut, but because *dull chisels lie*. They don't return enough information to learn from.

The same shape applies everywhere. A factor model with unclean input data lies — it generates returns whose attribution is muddled, so you can't tell whether the model worked or whether you got lucky. A horse who's been pushed past the point of attention lies — he'll perform exercises mechanically even when the underlying balance is wrong, so you can't tell whether your aids are clean. A debugger whose output is buried in irrelevant log lines lies — the actual bug's signature is invisible in the noise.

In every case, the *first* improvement isn't about doing the thing better. It's about getting the feedback channel clean enough that doing the thing can compound. Craftsmen know this. Quants relearn it every few years. Trainers (good ones) treat it as the foundation. Programmers tend to underestimate it until they've burned a week on a bug that better logging would have made trivial.

**Generalised version**: the rate at which any skill compounds is bounded by the quality of the feedback channel. Improving the channel produces gains that look exponential because every subsequent practice session converts to learning more efficiently.

**Concrete daily practice**: when starting a new project, spend the first day on instrumentation. When starting work with a new horse, spend the first sessions establishing communication. When taking on a new analyst, spend the first month on shared definitions of what "good" looks like. This always feels like wasted time and is always the highest-leverage time in the project.

**The shadow side**: people who never invest in feedback channels can still produce work, but their growth flattens early. They mistake "I've been doing this 20 years" for expertise. Twenty years of muddied feedback ≠ twenty years of compounding improvement.

title: Why I distrust closed taxonomies
body:
# Why I distrust closed taxonomies

A perennial source of trouble in finance: the idea that the world divides cleanly into pre-named categories. Asset classes. Investment strategies. Risk factors. The taxonomies pretend to be the structure of the territory, but they're the structure of last decade's *understanding* of the territory.

Closed taxonomies have a specific failure mode: they push thinking into the categories you have rather than the ones you'd need. Once your reporting line says "this strategy is a momentum strategy," you start defending its momentum-ness rather than asking what it actually does. The label colonises the work.

Open taxonomies — fuzzy categories, hybrid descriptors, multi-axis labels — are uglier and harder to work with. They don't fit cleanly in databases. They confuse new joiners. They're also closer to true. The strategies that produce real returns over decades tend to be hybrids that don't fit neatly anywhere — and the labels we eventually invent for them ("trend-following with carry," "convexity-tilted relative-value") are awkward exactly because they cross category lines.

**Connection to interpretability**: the SAE-vs-geometry argument is the same shape. SAEs assume the underlying concept space is *cleanly partitioned* into discrete features. The empirical evidence is that real concept space is full of nonlinear coupled structures — circles, helices, shells. Imposing a partition tells you what the partition allows you to see, and hides everything else.

**Connection to riding**: every dressage test is a closed taxonomy of "movements." Real horsemanship lives in the transitions between them. The judging system has to award marks for movements because that's measurable; the actual quality of riding lives in the un-judgeable spaces. Caspian doesn't think of his work as a sequence of movements. He thinks (or whatever the equivalent is) in terms of balance, rhythm, attention. The taxonomy isn't his.

**The discipline this implies**: when picking up any new field, ask "what are the official categories" — *and then* ask "what work falls between or across them." That's where the unclaimed value usually is. Often the categories were drawn at a moment when the field was in a particular state, and the world has moved on but the categories haven't.

The cost of this discipline is that you sound vague to people whose career is built on the official taxonomies. The reward is occasionally seeing things others can't.

title: The shape of a long bet
body:
# The shape of a long bet

A bet you'll know the outcome of in six months has a different shape from a bet you'll know in ten years. Six-month bets compound feedback fast — you make many, learn quickly which heuristics work, the loop is tight. Ten-year bets compound differently — you make few, the feedback is slow and contaminated by everything else that happens, and the bet's quality is more about its *internal coherence* than about your live calibration.

Most career-defining decisions are ten-year bets. Most professional skill is built on six-month bets. There's a misalignment.

**What helps for long bets that doesn't help for short bets**:
- Pre-registering what would convince you you were wrong. (Six-month bets, you'll just see the answer. Ten-year bets, you'll rationalise around any outcome unless you wrote down the falsifier in advance.)
- Worrying about your motivations more than your reasoning. (Reasoning errors get caught by feedback in short bets. In long bets, motivated reasoning is the dominant failure mode and there's no live correction.)
- Optionality over conviction. (A long bet that doesn't admit course correction is a coin flip with extra steps. A long bet structured as a sequence of revisable smaller bets is a learning system.)

**What helps for short bets that hurts long bets**:
- Confidence calibration based on recent track record. (Recent record on six-month bets says nothing useful about a ten-year bet's quality.)
- Adjusting strategy based on intermediate signals. (Intermediate signals on long bets are usually noise that triggers panic.)

**Connection to investing**: the conflation of these two horizons is the most common mistake in junior PMs. Treating a five-year-thesis position with the same risk discipline as a five-day trade either over-trades the conviction position or under-trades the short-cycle one. The temporal horizon is the dominant variable; the strategy wrapper is secondary.

**Connection to relationships**: the same dynamic applies. Daily interactions are short-cycle bets — fast feedback, course-correctable. Long-term commitments are long-cycle bets where the live feedback is mostly noise and the quality lives in the structural fit you established at the start. Mistaking one for the other is how good marriages collapse over small things and bad ones survive on momentum.

**For the project list**: the geodesic-retrieval bet is sitting in an awkward space. The empirical falsifier is short-cycle (ship the bench, see if numbers land). The framing is long-cycle (geometry as a primitive). Need to keep these horizons clearly separated in the work or one will eat the other.

title: Notes on Stoic exposure therapy
body:
# Notes on Stoic exposure therapy

Reading Hadot's *Philosophy as a Way of Life* alongside Marcus Aurelius for the third time, with one particular thread in mind: the Stoic *praemeditatio malorum* — the deliberate rehearsal of misfortunes.

The standard read of this is that it's about emotional preparation: imagine the loss, so the actual loss is less devastating. Marcus on his son's death, etc. There's something to that.

But re-reading with a quant's brain on, I think the practice does something more specific: *it generates synthetic data points outside your normal experiential distribution.* Most lived experience is in-distribution. The stoic exercise deliberately samples from the tails. The point isn't only emotional — it's epistemic. You're improving your model of your own reactions by sampling regions of state-space your daily life doesn't visit.

This is structurally identical to backtesting strategies on *out-of-distribution* historical data. A strategy backtested only on the 2010s is a strategy with no information about 2008-style stress. Forcing the backtest to include 2008 (and 1998, and 1973) is the praemeditatio of strategy design — synthetic-but-grounded sampling of stress regimes that the live trader hasn't seen.

The Stoics weren't doing it for risk-management reasons (they had different motivations), but the *function* of the practice is the same: extending the operating envelope of your own decision-making by rehearsing conditions that aren't currently present.

**Practical**: my own praemeditatio practice is mostly accidental and would be more useful if I made it deliberate. Currently I do it spontaneously when reading about other people's disasters — what would I have done in their shoes? It would be more rigorous to schedule it: once a quarter, an hour spent imagining specific concrete stress scenarios (Meridian losing a major LP, Caspian becoming permanently lame, my partner Robin becoming chronically ill, my own loss of cognitive function), and walking through the response in detail.

The goal isn't to depress oneself. It's to *de-rehearse the shock*. When something approximating a rehearsed scenario actually happens, the freeze-and-panic phase is shorter because some of the cognitive work is already done.

**Connection to riding**: Priya makes us do this with horse-related emergencies. *"What do you do if Caspian rears under saddle?"* — walked through twice a year, kept fresh. I've never had to use it. Means nothing about whether the practice was wasted; means the rehearsal worked.

title: Meridian Capital — book overview
body:
# Meridian Capital — book overview

Refresher for new joiners. Meridian runs a multi-strategy book across four desks. I sit on the systematic equity desk; this note is my mental model of the whole shop.

**Equity systematic** (my desk). Mid-frequency factor portfolio, rebalanced weekly. Standard factor exposures (value, momentum, quality, low-vol) with proprietary tilts on regime-conditional weighting. Capacity: ~$800m. Sharpe target 1.4.

**Macro discretionary**. Smaller team, higher conviction. Trades rates, FX, commodity term structure. Lower turnover, longer holding periods. The book most exposed to regime change — they print or bleed depending on whether the macro environment cooperates. Capacity bigger than equity but more episodic.

**Credit relative-value**. Fixed-income arb across cash bonds, CDS, and synthetic structures. Profits from temporary mispricings between related instruments. Sharpe tends to be very high in calm markets, brutal in stress. Tail-dependence problem: when correlations break down, the entire book moves the wrong way at once.

**Volatility / tail-risk**. Long convexity, structurally negative carry, designed to print when everything else is failing. Acts as a P&L hedge for the rest of the firm. Bleed in calm markets, save the year in stress events.

**Allocation logic**: the firm-level allocator weights desks based on a regime-conditional view. Calm regime → more credit RV, less tail. Stress regime → more tail, less credit. The interesting thing about this allocation framework is that it's *itself* a model that can be wrong about regime detection. The meta-risk is the regime model going stale.

**What I keep coming back to**: the book is structurally robust because each desk fails in different conditions. No single regime kills the firm. But if the desks become *correlated* in their failure modes (e.g., all desks underperform in a liquidity crunch), the structure collapses. That's the non-obvious tail risk: not individual desk drawdowns, but correlation-of-drawdowns.

Same shape as horse training, weirdly. A horse that knows ten exercises is robust if the exercises fail in different conditions; brittle if they all collapse under the same kind of pressure.

title: Tail dependence in commodity carry
body:
# Tail dependence in commodity carry

Reading Patton's copula textbook again. The recurring practical problem in our commodity carry book is that linear correlations look fine right up until they don't, and then they're catastrophically wrong.

**The setup**: long backwardated commodities, short contangoed ones. Carries positive on average. Linear correlation with broad equity markets is roughly 0.1 — looks like a clean diversifier. The pitch deck loves it.

**The reality**: in the bottom 5% of equity returns, the correlation isn't 0.1. It's 0.7. The strategy *appears* uncorrelated until the moment when uncorrelation would actually matter, then collapses into the same trade as everyone else. This is tail dependence in action. The Pearson correlation is a single number that averages over the whole joint distribution; it tells you nothing about whether the worst quintile of one variable is informative about the other.

**The diagnostic**: compute conditional probability that strategy returns are below the 5th percentile *given* equity returns are below the 5th percentile. If that conditional probability is materially above 5%, you have tail dependence regardless of what the linear correlation says. For our commodity book, it sits around 30%.

**Why this matters operationally**: portfolio construction tools default to mean-variance optimisation under Gaussian assumptions. The optimiser will happily allocate to a tail-dependent strategy because it sees a low correlation and a positive Sharpe and concludes "diversification." It can't see the conditional structure. So the portfolio looks great in normal times and falls apart in crises — exactly when diversification was supposed to save you.

**Calibration parallel**: this is the same problem as a probe that distinguishes truthful and confabulated outputs in calm conditions but breaks under adversarial prompting. The probe and the truth-detector have *good* unconditional performance — bad *conditional* performance under stress. The diagnostic that matters isn't average performance; it's worst-quintile performance.

**Action item**: revise the regime-conditional copula model. The current one assumes a Clayton copula in the lower tail. Empirical fit suggests we should be using a t-copula with low df — fatter tails on both sides. Estimated parameters logged in the desk repo.

title: Regime change detection — notes
body:
# Regime change detection — notes

Notes from this morning's research session. The systematic equity desk needs a tighter regime detector. The current one — a Markov-switching model on rolling realised vol — is too lagged. By the time it flags a regime change, the change has been ongoing for two weeks and we've already taken the drawdown.

**Three competing approaches I've tested**:

1. **Bayesian online changepoint detection** (Adams & MacKay). Lightweight, gives a posterior over "time since last changepoint." Catches changes faster than Markov-switching. Downside: very noisy on small samples; prone to flagging spurious changes during single-day vol spikes.

2. **Multivariate state-space model with Kalman filter on factor returns**. Catches changes that show up as factor-correlation shifts before they show up in volatility. Works well in backtests. Hideously expensive to estimate online.

3. **Embedding-based**: encode market state as a vector via a pretrained financial language model (sentiment + news + price action), use distance from rolling-mean state vector as a regime-change signal. Surprisingly competitive on backtests. Not robust to the model's training cutoff — degrades fast on novel regimes.

**What I keep noticing**: each method has a different *failure mode* for regime change. The first is too noisy, the second is too slow, the third is brittle to novelty. None is dominant. Combining them with a Bayesian model average actually beats any single one — the wisdom-of-the-ensemble effect.

**Conceptual parallel**: this maps cleanly onto the way Caspian's gait changes during long sessions. There are at least three signals — breathing, contact, footfall cadence — each of which independently is noisy or lagged, but combined give me a reliable read on his state changes. The principle is the same: regime change in a high-dimensional system is best detected by a heterogeneous ensemble of weak signals, not by tuning a single strong one.

**Open question**: when we deploy the ensemble in production next month, what's the right way to *down-weight* a member when its failure mode is active? An adaptive weight is the obvious answer but introduces a meta-regime-detection problem (how do we detect that one of our regime detectors is currently broken?). At some point the meta-meta tower has to terminate. Probably with a circuit breaker.

title: Factor decay benchmarks
body:
# Factor decay benchmarks

Quarterly review of factor performance against the regime-conditional model. The headline finding is the value factor's information coefficient has decayed materially since 2024 — we're now operating at roughly half the historical IC.

**Decay signature**: not an abrupt break (that would be a regime change). It's a slow erosion — the same trades pay less, work less reliably, get crowded faster. Classic alpha decay. Likely cause: factor information has been progressively absorbed into systematic flows from the larger ETF complex, leaving us with less unique signal.

**Three responses we're debating**:

1. **Increase rotation speed**. If the slow-form factor is decaying, harvest the faster-rotating residual. Risk: transaction costs eat the gain. We've estimated the breakeven turnover at roughly 4× current. Painful but plausible.

2. **Migrate to less-crowded factors**. The "quality" factor has been less discovered than value. But once we shift, we're a few quarters into riding the same decay curve. It's a temporary fix, not a structural one.

3. **Add a non-traditional factor**. Looking at signals derived from earnings call transcripts, supply-chain text, alt-data signatures. Higher orthogonality to existing factors but enormous data-quality issues. Long ramp-up.

**The structural reality**: any factor that's discoverable is eventually discovered, and once discovered, decays. The half-life of factor edges has been monotonically falling for two decades. A sustainable systematic equity book has to be *constantly* generating new factor candidates, not just optimising existing ones.

**Connection back**: this is the same dynamic as in horse training — once Caspian "knows" an exercise, the exercise stops generating learning. The training has to keep introducing structurally novel demands or the rate of progression flattens. Same compounding curve, same decay shape, same answer: keep finding new edges.

**What I keep underestimating** is how predictable this is in retrospect and how invisible it is in real time. The decay is gradual enough to rationalise as bad luck for two quarters. By quarter three, the regime is fully different and you've been running on conviction instead of data.

title: Rotation cost vs alpha tradeoff memo
body:
# Rotation cost vs alpha tradeoff memo

Memo for the desk allocator. We're carrying too much rotation cost relative to expected alpha on the mid-cap sleeve. Math:

Current sleeve characteristics:
- Annualised gross alpha estimate: 380 bp
- Annualised turnover: 380%
- Effective transaction cost (impact + spread + market-on-close fees): ~95 bp on the turnover
- **Net alpha after costs: ~285 bp**

Optimal-frontier reweighting (lower-turnover variant):
- Annualised gross alpha estimate: 290 bp
- Annualised turnover: 180%
- Effective transaction cost: ~45 bp
- **Net alpha after costs: ~245 bp**

The high-turnover variant *appears* to dominate on net alpha. But two things mute that conclusion. First, the transaction cost estimate at 380% turnover has a fat tail — actual costs in stress days are 2× the model. Second, the high-turnover variant has worse capacity (the same percentage degradation hits a smaller AUM range).

**Dynamic conclusion**: when AUM is below $400m, run the high-turnover variant. Above $400m, run the lower-turnover variant. The breakeven is sharper than the marginal-alpha math suggests because the impact cost component grows superlinearly with size.

**Meta-point**: we keep treating "alpha" as if it's intrinsic to the strategy. It's not. Alpha is conditional on the implementation regime — turnover, capacity, market depth. A strategy that produces 400 bp at $100m may produce 50 bp at $1B. The strategy is the same; the alpha is a function of how you run it.

**Same shape elsewhere**: in horse training, the "training value" of an exercise is conditional on the horse's current state, the time of session, the previous exercise sequence. Same exercise on a fresh horse produces something completely different from the same exercise on a tired one. We never write down "this drill produces 380 basis points of training value" because we know it's nonsensical without the conditional structure. We should have similar humility about strategy alpha.

title: Crucible — system overview
body:
# Crucible — system overview

The personal task / decision tracking system I've been building on weekends. Half because I needed it; half because building it teaches me more about distributed systems than reading would. Started in late 2024.

**What it does**: stores tasks, decisions, and evidence as a graph. Each task can carry one or more *assumptions* (things that need to be true for it to succeed); each assumption has a falsifier and a resolution event. The graph evolves as outcomes come in, propagating updates to dependent tasks. Local-first storage, optional sync to a personal server.

**Architecture**:
- **Storage**: SQLite with a small set of carefully-chosen tables. Tasks, assumptions, evidence events, and a graph edge table. Indexed for the queries I actually run.
- **Sync**: CRDT-based merging via `automerge`. Operates in the background; conflicts are rare because most edits are append-only.
- **CLI**: TypeScript. Single binary, no install dance. The CLI is the primary interface; the web UI is an afterthought.
- **Web UI**: lightweight React app, runs locally. Used for browsing, not entry.

**What I learned from building it**:
- Idempotency is the universal solvent. Every operation is structured so retrying it has no side effects. This made the sync layer about 100× simpler than designing it the first time without that constraint. Retrofitting idempotency later is hell.
- SQLite is genuinely enough for personal-scale data. The hours I'd have spent making Postgres work nicely were spent on actual product instead.
- The graph queries are where the value lives. Tasks-and-assumptions in isolation are a mediocre todo list. Tasks-and-assumptions *with their dependencies tracked* lets me see when an upstream falsifier resolves which downstream tasks become moot.

**Current limitations**:
- The CRDT merge handles 95% of cases beautifully and the remaining 5% require manual resolution. Acceptable for personal use; would not survive multi-user.
- No true multi-device offline. The sync is fine when devices are online; gets confused when one's been offline for a month.
- No real backup story. The local SQLite file is the source of truth; if I lose the laptop, I lose the data. Need to plug in a backup pipeline before scaling up.

**Why the geodesic-retrieval project matters for Crucible**: if the retrieval method works, Crucible's "find related tasks" feature gets dramatically more useful. Right now it's text-search-based and misses cross-domain connections (the same kind I notice when journaling).

title: Idempotency keys for write-safe APIs
body:
# Idempotency keys for write-safe APIs

Notes from refactoring Crucible's mutation API to use idempotency keys properly.
